topic: Day 1 · Hyperacute Imaging — CT, CTA, Perfusion & MRI
speakerBio: Reads hyperacute stroke scans and insists the first question is always the same one.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Your stroke-call patient is on the CT table at minute 20. The scan will answer three questions in sequence: Is there blood? Is there a big-vessel clot to pull? And is there still brain worth saving? Read them in that order and you will never thrombolyse a haemorrhage.

1 · The imaging logic

The first job of the scan is not to find the stroke — it is to exclude haemorrhage, because that single fact flips the treatment from thinning the blood to controlling the bleed.

2 · Non-contrast CT — fast, and it rules out blood

Available everywhere, seconds to acquire. Acute blood is hyperdense (white) immediately; acute ischaemia is subtle and early signs may be invisible for hours. Early ischaemic signs:

  • Hyperdense MCA sign — the clot itself, a bright artery.
  • Loss of grey–white differentiation and the insular ribbon sign.
  • Sulcal effacement from early oedema.
💡 ASPECTS

The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score divides the MCA territory into 10 regions and subtracts 1 for each showing early ischaemia (10 = normal). A score ≥6 generally means enough salvageable tissue to reperfuse; a low ASPECTS signals a large completed core that bleeds if you open it.

3 · CT angiography — find the clot to pull

A contrast bolus opacifies the arteries head-to-neck. CTA finds the large-vessel occlusion (LVO) — ICA, M1, proximal M2, basilar — that is the target for thrombectomy. It also assesses collaterals (good collaterals predict a bigger salvageable penumbra) and shows carotid disease and dissection.

4 · CT perfusion — is there brain worth saving?

MapMeaning
Tmax > 6 sDelayed tissue = the total hypoperfused volume (core + penumbra)
CBF < 30%The dead core
Mismatch (penumbra − core)Salvageable tissue — a large mismatch selects late-window patients for reperfusion

Perfusion imaging is what let DAWN and DEFUSE-3 extend thrombectomy to 6–24 hours: treat the physiology, not the clock.

5 · MRI / DWI — the most sensitive

  • Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) lights up within minutes of ischaemia — the most sensitive test for acute infarct.
  • DWI–FLAIR mismatch: a lesion bright on DWI but not yet on FLAIR is <~4.5 hours old — used to treat wake-up strokes of unknown onset (WAKE-UP trial).
  • MRI also best shows brainstem/posterior fossa strokes CT misses.

6 · The pathway in one line

🧭 Sequence

Non-contrast CT (blood? early core/ASPECTS) → CTA (LVO? collaterals?) → CT perfusion (mismatch, especially if late/wake-up). MRI/DWI when the diagnosis or timing is uncertain. Do not let imaging delay treatment in a clear early-window case — CT then needle.

☠️ M&M — the "ischaemic" stroke that was blood

A rushed team read a subtle non-contrast CT as ischaemia and gave thrombolysis; the hyperdensity they dismissed as artefact was a small deep haemorrhage, which the lytic turned into a fatal bleed. Lesson: the first and non-negotiable question of every stroke scan is "is there blood?" Acute haemorrhage is white and obvious — never rush past it to reach the treatment you were hoping to give.

7 · Take-home

  • CT first to exclude blood — everything downstream depends on it.
  • ASPECTS ≥6 = salvageable; CTA finds the LVO for thrombectomy.
  • Perfusion mismatch selects late-window and wake-up patients — physiology beats the clock.
  • DWI is most sensitive; DWI–FLAIR mismatch dates the unknown-onset stroke.

moderatorQs.q: What is the single most important question on the first stroke scan?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Is there blood? Acute haemorrhage is hyperdense and obvious on non-contrast CT, and its presence completely reverses management — from thinning the blood to controlling the bleed and the pressure. Only once haemorrhage is excluded do you look for early ischaemic change, ASPECTS, and then vessel and perfusion imaging.

moderatorQs.q: How did perfusion imaging change who we can treat?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It shifted late-window selection from time to tissue. Mapping a small dead core (CBF <30%) against a larger penumbra (Tmax >6 s), a favourable mismatch identifies patients who still benefit from thrombectomy out to 24 hours — exactly what DAWN and DEFUSE-3 proved.

moderatorQs.q: When is MRI worth the extra time?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: When diagnosis or timing is uncertain. DWI is the most sensitive test for early ischaemia and superior for posterior-fossa and small strokes CT misses. The DWI–FLAIR mismatch dates an unknown-onset or wake-up stroke — bright on DWI but not yet on FLAIR means likely within 4.5 hours and thrombolysable (WAKE-UP).

audienceQs.q: What is ASPECTS telling the team?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It quantifies how much MCA territory is already infarcted on baseline CT: 10 regions, minus one each for early ischaemic change (10 = normal). A score ≥6 generally supports reperfusion; a low ASPECTS warns of a large completed core likely to bleed if reperfused.

audienceQs.q: CTA adds contrast and time — is it always needed?
audienceQs.answerHTML: For any moderate-to-severe stroke, yes — it finds the large-vessel occlusion that is the thrombectomy target and shows collaterals, carotid disease and dissection. Skipping CTA is how LVOs go unreferred; done in the same session it adds little to door-to-needle time and changes management whenever a proximal clot is present.
